analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Pharmalabs is a fast grower in the India API/CDMO space with a compelling 30.6% net profit CAGR and a PEG of ~0.96 — just inside my buy zone. However, a massive capex surge to ₹444 Cr in FY25 has turned FCF negative and drained cash to just ₹7 Cr, so the story needs the capacity build-out to pay off before this becomes a ten-bagger candidate.
key_strengths: Earnings growing 30.6% CAGR with PEG ~0.96 (P/E 29.3 / ~30% growth) — right at my sweet spot
EBITDA margins expanding (₹198 Cr → ₹473 Cr) with low D/E of 0.33 — financial discipline intact
Diversified API portfolio + CDMO services taps secular India pharma outsourcing wave
key_risks: FY25 FCF swung to -₹112 Cr on ₹444 Cr capex — cash pile collapsed to just ₹7 Cr, no margin of safety
Borrowings nearly doubled (₹285 → ₹659 Cr balance sheet) in one year — debt load could crimp future earnings
Revenue dipped in FY24 (₹1,945 → ₹1,853 Cr) showing the growth story is not yet linear — execution risk on new capacity
red_flags: Free cash flow negative in FY25 (-₹112 Cr) with capex 2x prior year — heavy bet on unproven capacity
Cash at ₹7 Cr is dangerously thin; any revenue shortfall forces dilution or expensive borrowing
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aarti Pharmalabs checks the core Lynch boxes for a fast grower: 20.8% revenue CAGR, 30.6% net profit CAGR, and a PEG of roughly 0.96 — just below my 1.0 threshold. The CDMO angle is the real story here; India is taking global API market share and contract manufacturing is a capital-light, repeat-revenue model once established. Operating margins are expanding steadily and the D/E of 0.33 shows management hasn't been reckless — until FY25.

The FY25 capex of ₹444 Cr (more than 2x the prior year) is the central question mark. That level of investment — with cash near zero and borrowings surging — tells me management is either making a bold, well-timed capacity bet for export/CDMO contracts, or overreaching. I need to see FY26 revenue accelerate above 25% to validate this spend; if growth stays at 20% on a much larger asset base, returns will compress and the story weakens. Until the new capacity is absorbed into earnings, I'd hold rather than add — but this is not a name to sell outright given the underlying growth trajectory.
